questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the main work a prologue does before the action starts
questions.stem: In my observing log I copied the opening speech of the village drama and labelled it exposition; what is that speech chiefly for?

options.text: It hands the audience the facts and situation they need before the play's action begins
options.misconception: treats a prologue as decorative mood with no factual work

options.text: It hides the central conflict so the audience must piece the premise together unaided
options.misconception: believes a prologue always withholds the premise

options.text: It establishes the voice of the chorus as a separate commenting body
options.misconception: confuses the prologue's job with the chorus's job

options.text: It reveals the ending in advance so the audience knows what awaits the hero
options.misconception: assumes every prologue previews the final outcome

questions.explanation: A prologue delivers exposition, giving the audience the facts and situation before the plot turns. It neither previews the ending nor speaks for a chorus, so B, C and D misstate its purpose.
questions.hint: Think about what the audience needs before the first scene.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a chorus's vantage point enlarges what an audience can know
questions.stem: Reading the chorus's speech in my theatre club's script, I wondered why it seems to know events it never witnessed; explain the advantage a chorus gives an audience.

answer.exemplar: A chorus occupies a position outside the characters' actions: it stands apart, observes, comments, and can report on what happened away from the stage. That outside vantage lets it hold two truths at once, what the audience sees and what the characters do not, so the audience learns the wider context, the consequences, and the moral or ironic judgement on the action at the same time.

questions.explanation: The chorus stands outside the action, so it can hold the whole picture and comment on it. Its vantage is neither a participant's nor an ordinary spectator's, letting it reveal context and irony the characters lack.
questions.hint: Consider what a voice outside the action can see.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Blank verse as a register signal
questions.learningObjective: Explain what unrhymed iambic pentameter signals about a scene's register
questions.stem: Transcribing the noble's speech for my log, I noticed the lines run long without rhyme; explain what that verse form tells the audience.

answer.exemplar: Unrhymed iambic pentameter signals formality and gravity: the line keeps a steady classical measure while dispensing with rhyme, so the language sounds elevated and measured rather than conversational. In a play that also uses prose, blank verse becomes a register marker, letting the audience hear at once that a character is speaking with authority, ceremony, or elevated feeling, and that a shift into prose marks a drop into the everyday.

questions.explanation: Blank verse keeps a formal metrical line without rhyme, which reads as elevated and controlled. Used beside prose, it marks register shifts, so the audience hears when a character steps out of the everyday.
questions.hint: Compare the speeches around it: some are in prose.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the function of an unresolved ending in a problem play
questions.stem: After our reading of the play where a suitor must choose between love and a title, I wrote that it refuses to settle its own dispute; explain what that refusal is designed to do.

answer.exemplar: The play's unresolved ending turns a private choice into a public question. By refusing to show the suitor rewarded or punished, it denies the audience the comfort of a moral verdict and leaves the conflict legible as a clash of values: affection against estate, private choice against public duty. The audience leaves holding the argument rather than a verdict, which is the design of a problem play rather than a failure of the plot to close.

questions.explanation: A problem play stages a dilemma and withholds the verdict so the audience must weigh the values at stake. The open ending is the method, not a plot that failed to close.
questions.hint: Ask who is left to settle the dispute after the play.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a mixed cast lets unlike logics collide
questions.stem: In the play where a prophet, a beggar, and a king all argue over a marriage, I wondered why the stage can hold them together; explain the convention at work.

answer.exemplar: The play asks its audience to accept a stage wide enough for divine, human, and marginal figures at once, and the convention works by promising that each order speaks under its own logic. The prophet measures everything by fate, the beggar by appetite and survival, the king by custom and interest. Because the play licenses their meeting, the audience judges them against one another rather than against ordinary expectation, and the collisions expose how each order defines what matters.

questions.explanation: A mixed cast works because the play licenses incompatible orders of being into one frame, letting each speak by its own logic. The collisions then test those logics against one another, which is what the scene is built to expose.
questions.hint: Consider what each kind of figure measures value by.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why even-handed argument serves a problem play
questions.stem: I wrote that the second act of the play argues both sides so evenly that nobody could choose; explain why that is the design rather than a failure.

answer.exemplar: Even-handed argument is the design of a problem play because the play's subject is a question that the plot cannot answer without taking a side the dramatist does not hold. By letting each position carry its strongest case, the play transfers the decision to the audience: the tension does not depend on a hidden answer but on the pressure of two reasonable demands, each of which would cost something real. A dramatist who closed the question would end the argument rather than hand it on.

questions.explanation: Even-handedness keeps the question genuinely open, because settling it would require a verdict the play does not hold. The pressure of competing reasonable demands is the subject, and the audience is left to decide.
questions.hint: Consider what a verdict would have to assume.

answer.exemplar: A well-made plot expects the resolution to grow out of what the audience has already watched: the causes must be laid earlier, so the ending is the consequence of the action rather than an interruption of it. questions.learningObjective: Explain what printing two endings does to a play's argument

answer.exemplar: Printing two endings makes the question the play's subject rather than its ornament. questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the effect of giving the audience the outcome early
questions.stem: I noted that the audience is told early exactly which character will be punished, and by the end the play has explained why; what is the effect?

options.text: The audience is deprived of the pleasure of not knowing
options.misconception: assumes foreknowledge is always a defect

options.text: The audience is spared the strain of following the cause chain
options.misconception: credits convenience where suspense was intended

options.text: The audience is asked to watch for the proof rather than the outcome
options.misconception: reads foreknowledge as removing the outcome entirely

options.text: The audience can watch the causes accumulate and judge the fit

questions.explanation: Telling the audience the outcome early invites them to watch the causes accumulate and judge the fit, a deliberate use of foreknowledge. It spoils no pleasure and removes no strain, so A, B and C misread it.
questions.hint: Consider what the audience is left to watch for.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Blank verse as a register signal
questions.learningObjective: Interpret prose spoken inside a verse play
questions.stem: Our actor used prose for the fool throughout the play and the audience noticed the difference; what does that choice register?

options.text: A character who stands outside the formal world the verse creates
A character who has not learned the verse the other characters use
options.misconception: turns a register choice into a claim about education

options.text: A character whose lines the dramatist wrote later than the rest
options.misconception: invents a production history the play does not support

options.text: A character who is meant to sound less intelligent than the others
options.misconception: confuses register with intelligence

questions.explanation: Prose in a verse world marks a character who stands outside its formal order, which is why the fool sounds like commentary from elsewhere. It implies no untrained ear, no rewriting, and no lesser intelligence, so B, C and D misread it.
questions.hint: Consider what prose does inside a verse play.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Read the closing sentence of an opening speech for its function

stimulus.body: The speaker announces that the house in question has stood empty for nine years, that two families claim it, and that the argument about it is about to be heard again in court. The speaker then adds that nothing in the speech is meant to settle the matter.

questions.stem: I wrote this into my log as a model of delivered exposition; what does the closing sentence do?

options.text: It announces that the speech itself will not decide the dispute
options.misconception: hears a disclaimer about the speech, not the coming trial

options.text: It warns the audience that the court scene will be badly acted
options.misconception: reads a thematic disclaimer as a production note

options.text: It invites the audience to treat the coming trial as unresolved business
options.misconception: mistakes an invitation for a summary of the play's verdict

options.text: It confirms that the families will settle the matter out of court
options.misconception: turns an open question into a promised ending

questions.explanation: The closing sentence tells the audience to expect a question rather than a verdict, keeping the coming trial as open business. It decides nothing and promises no settlement, so A, B and D misread it.
questions.hint: Consider the register the sentence sets for what follows.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how tense places a chorus after the events
questions.stem: I asked why the chorus speaks in the past tense about events the audience has just seen; explain what the tense does.

answer.exemplar: The past tense marks the chorus as a voice that has already lived through and survived what it describes. Speaking from a position after the fact, it can treat events as settled history and can name their meaning, which no character on stage is able to do at the time. The tense therefore gives the commentary an authority of hindsight: it does not participate in the crisis but reads it, and the audience hears the difference between being inside an event and knowing how it ended.

questions.explanation: The past tense places the chorus after the events, giving it the authority of hindsight and letting it name meaning the characters cannot. The commentary reads the crisis from outside it rather than joining in.
questions.hint: Consider where the speaker of that tense stands.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify what the presence of a dead figure makes arguable
questions.stem: Our set put the dead father at the table with the living family; what does the convention of that presence buy the play?

options.text: A clash between claims the living cannot settle without the dead
A chance for the audience to see how the family behaves when unwatched
options.misconception: reduces the ghost to a device for observing behaviour

options.text: A way to keep the character from being forgotten by the playwright
options.misconception: reads the convention as authorial insurance

options.text: A proof that the family are dishonest about the father's death
options.misconception: turns a presence into a verdict on the family

questions.explanation: Putting the dead at the table lets claims the living cannot settle be argued in one frame, so the presence generates conflict rather than resolving it. It is not surveillance, insurance, or a verdict, so B, C and D misread it.
questions.hint: Consider what becomes arguable once he is present.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Comedy of manners and its target
questions.learningObjective: Weigh competing accounts of what a satire attacks
questions.stem: My final note asked whether the farce's target is the court, the suitors, or the custom both serve; which reading best fits?

options.text: The custom alone, since the courtiers merely follow it without choosing
options.misconception: removes the agents from the satire

options.text: The custom as practised by people who profit from it and would defend it
The suitors alone, since the courtiers appear only as their victims
options.misconception: pins the satire on one faction of characters

options.text: The court alone, since the suitors are given nothing to comment on
options.misconception: ignores the second group the play keeps satirising

questions.explanation: Manners comedy targets the custom as practised, since the play shows courtiers and suitors living by rules that flatter and protect them. Singling out one faction misses how the satire works on both, so A, C and D misplace it.
questions.hint: Consider who benefits from the rules being satirised.
